{{Short description|Concept in physics}}
In [[solid state physics]], the '''magnetic space groups''', or '''[[Alexei Vasilievich Shubnikov|Shubnikov]] groups''', are the [[symmetry group]]s which classify the symmetries of a crystal both in space, and in a two-valued property such as [[electron spin]]. To represent such a property, each lattice point is colored black or white,<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://www.scipress.org/journals/forma/pdf/1501/15010057.pdf|title=Black-and-White Symmetry, Magnetic Symmetry, Self-Duality and Antiprismatic Symmetry: The Common Mathematical Background|author=Gábor Gévay|journal=Forma|volume=15|pages=57–60|year=2000|archive-date=2021-11-20|access-date=2019-04-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211120025634/http://www.scipress.org/journals/forma/pdf/1501/15010057.pdf}}</ref> and in addition to the usual three-dimensional [[symmetry operation]]s, there is a so-called "antisymmetry" operation which turns all black lattice points white and all white lattice points black. Thus, the magnetic space groups serve as an extension to the [[crystallographic space group]]s which describe spatial symmetry alone.

The application of magnetic space groups to crystal structures is motivated by [[Curie's Principle]]. Compatibility with a material's symmetries, as described by the magnetic space group, is a necessary condition for a variety of material properties, including [[ferromagnetism]], [[ferroelectricity]], [[topological insulator|topological insulation]].

==History==

A major step was the work of [[Heinrich Heesch]], who first rigorously established the concept of antisymmetry as part of a series of papers in 1929 and 1930.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Heesch | first=H. |author-link=Heinrich Heesch| title=Zur Strukturtheorie der ebenen Symmetriegruppen |trans-title=Structure theory of plane symmetry groups| journal=Zeitschrift für Kristallographie - Crystalline Materials | volume=71 | issue=1–6 | date=1929-01-01 | issn=2196-7105 | doi=10.1524/zkri.1929.71.1.95 | pages=95–102| s2cid=102004261 |language=de}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last=Heesch | first=H. |author-link=Heinrich Heesch| title=Zur systematischen Strukturtheorie. II. |trans-title=Systematic structure theory II| journal=Zeitschrift für Kristallographie - Crystalline Materials | volume=72 | issue=1–6 | date=1930-01-01 | issn=2196-7105 | doi=10.1524/zkri.1930.72.1.177 | pages=177–201| s2cid=101972126 |language=de}}</ref><ref name="Heesch1930">{{cite journal|last1=Heesch|first1=H.|author-link=Heinrich Heesch|title=Zur systematischen Strukturtheorie. III - Über die vierdimensionalen Gruppen des dreidimensionalen Raumes|trans-title=Systematic Structure theory III - On the four-dimensional groups of three-dimensional space|journal=Zeitschrift für Kristallographie - Crystalline Materials|volume=73|issue=1–6|year=1930|issn=2196-7105|doi=10.1524/zkri.1930.73.1.325|pages=325–345|s2cid=102161514|language=de}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last=Heesch | first=H. |author-link=Heinrich Heesch| title=Zur systematischen Strukturtheorie. IV - Über die Symmetrien zweiter Art in Kontinuen und Remidiskontinuen
|trans-title=Systematic structure theory IV - On the symmetry of the second kind in continua and semicontinua| journal=Zeitschrift für Kristallographie - Crystalline Materials | volume=73 | issue=1–6 | date=1930-01-01 | issn=2196-7105 | doi=10.1524/zkri.1930.73.1.346 | pages=346–356| s2cid=102161512 |language=de}}</ref> Applying this antisymmetry operation to the 32 [[crystallographic point group]]s gives a total of 122 magnetic point groups.<ref name="Wills2017">{{cite journal|last1=Wills|first1=Andrew S.|title=A historical introduction to the symmetries of magnetic structures. Part 1. Early quantum theory, neutron powder diffraction and the coloured space groups|journal=Powder Diffraction|volume=32|issue=2|year=2017|pages=148–155|issn=0885-7156|doi=10.1017/S0885715617000124|arxiv=1609.09666|bibcode=2017PDiff..32..148W|s2cid=118533941}}</ref><ref name="PantuluRadhakrishna1967">{{cite journal|last1=Pantulu|first1=P. V.|last2=Radhakrishna|first2=S.|title=A method of deriving shubnikov groups|journal=Proceedings of the Indian Academy of Sciences A|volume=66|issue=2|year=1967|pages=107–111|issn=0370-0089|doi=10.1007/BF03049452|s2cid=118874086|url=https://www.ias.ac.in/article/fulltext/seca/066/02/0107-0111|url-access=subscription}}</ref> However, although Heesch correctly laid out each of the magnetic point groups, his work remained obscure, and the point groups were later re-derived by Tavger and Zaitsev.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=B.A.|last1=Tavger|first2=V.M. |last2=Zaitsev|title=Magnetic Symmetry of Crystals |journal=Journal of Experimental and Theoretical Physics|year=1956|volume=3|issue=3|page=430|url=http://jetp.ac.ru/cgi-bin/dn/e_003_03_0430.pdf}}</ref> The concept was more fully explored by Shubnikov in terms of [[Dichromatic symmetry|color symmetry]].<ref>{{cite book|author1=A. V. Shubnikov|author2=N. V. Belov|title=[[Colored Symmetry (book)|Colored Symmetry]]|year=1964|publisher=New York, Macmillan}}</ref> When applied to space groups, the number increases from the usual 230 three dimensional space groups to 1651 magnetic space groups,<ref name="Grimmer2009">{{cite journal|last1=Grimmer|first1=Hans|title=Comments on tables of magnetic space groups|journal=Acta Crystallographica Section A|volume=65|issue=2|year=2009|pages=145–155|issn=0108-7673|doi=10.1107/S0108767308039007|pmid=19225196|bibcode=2009AcCrA..65..145G|url=https://www.dora.lib4ri.ch/psi/islandora/object/psi%3A17243}}</ref> as found in the 1953 thesis of [[Alexander Mihailovich Zamorzaev|Alexandr Zamorzaev]].<ref>{{cite thesis|author=Zamorzaev, A. M. |year=1953|language=Russian|title=Generalization of the Fedorov groups|type=PhD|publisher=[[Saint Petersburg State University|Leningrad State University]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|journal=Kristallografiya|title=Generalization of the Fedorov groups|volume=2|pages=15–20|year=1957}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Generalization of the Fedorov groups|journal=Soviet Physics Crystallography| volume=2|pages=10–15}}</ref> While the magnetic space groups were originally found using geometry, it was later shown the same magnetic space groups can be found using [[Generating set of a group|generating sets]].<ref>{{cite journal | last=Kim | first=Shoon K. | title=The 38 assemblies of the general generator sets for 1421 magnetic double space groups | journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics | publisher=AIP Publishing | volume=27 | issue=5 | year=1986 | issn=0022-2488 | doi=10.1063/1.527397 | pages=1484–1489| bibcode=1986JMP....27.1484K }}</ref>

==Description==

===Magnetic space groups===
The magnetic space groups can be placed into three categories. First, the 230 colorless groups contain only spatial symmetry, and correspond to the crystallographic space groups. Then there are 230 grey groups, which are invariant under antisymmetry. Finally are the 1191 black-white groups, which contain the more complex symmetries. There are two common conventions for giving names to the magnetic space groups. They are Opechowski-Guccione (named after [[Wladyslaw Opechowski]] and Rosalia Guccione)<ref>{{cite book|title=Magnetism|volume=2A|editor-last1=Rado|editor-first1=George T.|editor-last2=Suhl|editor-first2=Harry|chapter=Magnetic Symmetry|author-last1=Opechowski|author-first1=W.|author-last2=Guccione|author-first2=R.|oclc=31184704|year=1965|publisher=Academic Press|location=New York}}</ref> and Belov-Neronova-Smirnova (named after Nikolay Vasilyevich Belov, Nina Nikolaevna Neronova and Tamara Serafimovna Smirnova, then Kuntsevich).<ref>{{cite journal | first1=N.V. | last1=Belov | first2=N. N. | last2=Neronova | first3=T. S. | last3=Smirnova | title=Shubnikov groups | journal=Soviet Physics Crystallography | publisher=American Institute of Physics | issn=0038-5638 | year=1957 | volume=2 | issue=3 | pages=311–322 | url=https://archive.org/details/crystallography-reports_may-june-1957_2_3/page/310/mode/2up |access-date=30 July 2025}}</ref><ref name="Grimmer2009" /> For colorless and grey groups, the conventions use the same names, but they treat the black-white groups differently. A full list of the magnetic space groups (in both conventions) can be found both in the original papers, and in several places online.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://stokes.byu.edu/iso/magneticspacegroups.php|title=ISO-MAG Table of Magnetic Space Groups|author1=Harold T. Stokes|author2=Branton J. Campbell|access-date=14 Apr 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cryst.ehu.es/cryst/msg_all.php|title=Magnetic Space Groups List|publisher=University of the Basque Country - Bilbao Crystallographic Server|access-date=14 Apr 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Magnetic Group Tables: 1-, 2-, and 3-Dimensional Magnetic Subperiodic Groups and Magnetic Space Groups|last1=Litvin|first1=D. B.|editor1-first=D. B|editor1-last=Litvin|year=2013|doi=10.1107/9780955360220001|isbn=978-0-9553602-2-0|publisher=International Union of Crystallography}}</ref>

The types can be distinguished by their different construction.<ref name=Bradley2010 /> Type I magnetic space groups, <math>\mathcal{M}_I</math> are identical to the ordinary space groups,<math>G</math>.

:<math>\mathcal{M}_I=G</math>

Type II magnetic space groups, <math>\mathcal{M}_{II}</math>, are made up of all the symmetry operations of the crystallographic space group, <math>G</math>, plus the product of those operations with time reversal operation, <math>\mathcal{T}</math>. Equivalently, this can be seen as the [[Direct product of groups|direct product]] of an ordinary space group with the point group <math>1'</math>.

:<math>\mathcal{M}_{II}=G + \mathcal{T}G</math>
:<math>\mathcal{M}_{II}=G \times 1'</math>

Type III magnetic space groups, <math>\mathcal{M}_{III}</math>, are constructed using a group <math>H</math>, which is a subgroup of <math>G</math> with [[Index of a subgroup|index]] 2.

:<math>\mathcal{M}_{III}=H + \mathcal{T} (G-H)</math>

Type IV magnetic space groups, <math>\mathcal{M}_{IV}</math>, are constructed with the use of a pure [[Translation (geometry)|translation]], <math>\{E|t_0\}</math>, which is Seitz notation<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Litvin | first1=Daniel B. | last2=Kopský | first2=Vojtěch | title=Seitz notation for symmetry operations of space groups | journal=Acta Crystallographica Section A | publisher=International Union of Crystallography (IUCr) | volume=67 | issue=4 | date=2011-05-26 | issn=0108-7673 | doi=10.1107/s010876731101378x | pages=415–418| pmid=21694481 | bibcode=2011AcCrA..67..415L }}</ref> for null rotation and a translation, <math>t_0</math>. Here the <math>t_0</math> is a vector (usually given in [[fractional coordinates]]) pointing from a black colored point to a white colored point, or vice versa.

:<math>\mathcal{M}_{IV}=G + \mathcal{T}\{E|t_0\}G</math>

===Magnetic point groups===

The following table lists all of the 122 possible three-dimensional magnetic point groups. This is given in the short version of [[Hermann–Mauguin notation]] in the following table. Here, the addition of an apostrophe to a symmetry operation indicates that the combination of the [[symmetry element]] and the antisymmetry operation is a symmetry of the structure. There are 32 [[Crystallographic point group]]s, 32 grey groups, and 58 magnetic point groups.<ref>{{cite book|title=Teaching crystallographic andmagnetic point group symmetry using three-dimensional rendered visualizations|url=https://www.iucr.org/__data/assets/pdf_file/0006/13929/final_23.pdf|first=Marc|last=DeGraef|access-date=2020-01-17}}</ref>

The magnetic point groups which are compatible with [[ferromagnetism]] are colored cyan, the magnetic point groups which are compatible with [[ferroelectricity]] are colored red, and the magnetic point groups which are compatible with both ferromagnetism and ferroelectricity are purple.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Schmid|first=Hans|title=On a magnetoelectric classification of materials|journal=International Journal of Magnetism|year=1973|volume=4|issue=4|pages=337–361|url=https://archive-ouverte.unige.ch/unige:32935}}</ref> There are 31 magnetic point groups which are compatible with [[ferromagnetism]]. These groups, sometimes called ''admissible'', leave at least one component of the spin invariant under operations of the point group. There are 31 point groups compatible with [[ferroelectricity]]; these are generalizations of the crystallographic [[polar point group]]s. There are also 31 point groups compatible with the theoretically proposed [[Toroidal moment|ferrotorodicity]]. Similar symmetry arguments have been extended to other electromagnetic material properties such as [[Magnetoelectric effect|magnetoelectricity]] or [[piezoelectricity]].<ref>{{cite journal | last=Schmid | first=Hans | title=Some symmetry aspects of ferroics and single phase multiferroics | journal=Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter | publisher=IOP Publishing | volume=20 | issue=43 | date=2008-10-09 | issn=0953-8984 | doi=10.1088/0953-8984/20/43/434201 | article-number=434201| bibcode=2008JPCM...20Q4201S | s2cid=120569385 }}</ref>

The following diagrams show the [[stereographic projection]] of most of the magnetic point groups onto a flat surface. Not shown are the grey point groups, which look identical to the ordinary crystallographic point groups, except they are also invariant under the antisymmetry operation.

===Black-white Bravais lattices===
The black-white Bravais lattices characterize the [[translational symmetry]] of the structure like the typical [[Bravais lattice]]s, but also contain additional symmetry elements. For black-white Bravais lattices, the number of black and white sites is always equal.<ref>{{cite book |editor-first=Antonios |editor-last=Gonis| editor-first2=Patrice E. A. |editor-last2=Turchi |first1=D. E. |last1=Laughlin|first2=M. A. |last2=Willard|first3=M. E. |last3=McHenry| title=Phase transformations and evolution in materials: proceedings of a symposium sponsored by the Alloy Phase Committee of the joint IMPMD/SMD of the Minerals, Metals, and Materials Society (TMS), held at the 2000 TMS Annual Meeting in Nashville, Tennessee, USA, March 12-16, 2000 | publisher=TMS | location=Warrendale, Pa | year=2000 | isbn=978-0-87339-468-0 | oclc=44883836 | pages=121–137|url=https://www.andrew.cmu.edu/user/dl0p/laughlin/pdf/252.pdf|chapter=Magnetic Ordering: Some Structural Aspects}}</ref> There are 14 traditional Bravais lattices, 14 grey lattices, and 22 black-white Bravais lattices, for a total of 50 two-color lattices in three dimensions.<ref name=Atoji>{{cite journal | last=Atoji | first=Masao | title=Graphical Representations of Magnetic Space Groups | journal=American Journal of Physics | publisher=American Association of Physics Teachers (AAPT) | volume=33 | issue=3 | year=1965 | issn=0002-9505 | doi=10.1119/1.1971375 | pages=212–219| bibcode=1965AmJPh..33..212A }}</ref>

The table shows the 36 black-white Bravais lattices, including the 14 traditional [[Bravais lattices]], but excluding the 14 gray lattices which look identical to the traditional lattices. The lattice symbols are those used for the traditional Bravais lattices. The suffix in the symbol indicates the mode of centering by the black (antisymmetry) points in the lattice, where ''s'' denotes edge centering.

===Magnetic superspace groups===
{{See also|Superstructure (condensed matter)}}

When the periodicity of the magnetic order coincides with the periodicity of crystallographic order, the magnetic phase is said to be ''commensurate'', and can be well-described by a magnetic space group. However, when this is not the case, the order does not correspond to any magnetic space group. These phases can instead be described by ''magnetic superspace groups'', which describe ''incommensurate'' order.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Perez-Mato | first1=J M | last2=Ribeiro | first2=J L | last3=Petricek | first3=V | last4=Aroyo | first4=M I | title=Magnetic superspace groups and symmetry constraints in incommensurate magnetic phases | journal=Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter | publisher=IOP Publishing | volume=24 | issue=16 | date=2012-03-26 | issn=0953-8984 | doi=10.1088/0953-8984/24/16/163201 | article-number=163201| pmid=22447842 |arxiv=1107.2358| bibcode=2012JPCM...24p3201P | s2cid=11738423 }}</ref> This is the same formalism often used to describe the ordering of some [[quasicrystal]]s.

==Phase transitions==
The [[Landau theory]] of second-order [[phase transition]]s has been applied to magnetic phase transitions. The magnetic space group of disordered structure, <math>G_0</math>, transitions to the magnetic space group of the ordered phase, <math>G_1</math>. <math>G_1</math> is a [[subgroup]] of <math>G_0</math>, and keeps only the symmetries which have not been broken during the phase transition. This can be tracked numerically by evolution of the [[order parameter]], which belongs to a single [[irreducible representation]] of <math>G_0</math>.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Dimmock | first=John O. | title=Use of Symmetry in the Determination of Magnetic Structures | journal=Physical Review | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=130 | issue=4 | date=1963-05-15 | issn=0031-899X | doi=10.1103/physrev.130.1337 | pages=1337–1344| bibcode=1963PhRv..130.1337D }}</ref>

Important magnetic phase transitions include the paramagnetic to ferromagnetic transition at the [[Curie temperature]] and the paramagnetic to [[Antiferromagnetism|antiferromagnetic]] transition at the [[Néel temperature]]. Differences in the magnetic phase transitions explain why [[Iron(III) oxide|Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>]], [[Manganese(II) carbonate|MnCO<sub>3</sub>]], and [[Cobalt(II) carbonate|CoCO<sub>3</sub>]] are weakly ferromagnetic, whereas the structurally similar [[Chromium(III) oxide|Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>]] and [[Iron(II) carbonate|FeCO<sub>3</sub>]] are purely antiferromagnetic.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Dzyaloshinsky | first=I. | title=A thermodynamic theory of "weak" ferromagnetism of antiferromagnetics | journal=Journal of Physics and Chemistry of Solids | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=4 | issue=4 | year=1958 | issn=0022-3697 | doi=10.1016/0022-3697(58)90076-3 | pages=241–255| bibcode=1958JPCS....4..241D }}</ref> This theory developed into what is now known as [[antisymmetric exchange]].

A related scheme is the classification of ''Aizu species'' which consist of a prototypical non-ferroic magnetic point group, the letter "F" for [[Ferroics|ferroic]], and a ferromagnetic or ferroelectric point group which is a subgroup of the prototypical group which can be reached by continuous motion of the atoms in the [[crystal structure]].<ref>{{cite journal | last=Aizu | first=Kêitsiro | title=Possible Species of Ferromagnetic, Ferroelectric, and Ferroelastic Crystals | journal=Physical Review B | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=2 | issue=3 | date=1970-08-01 | issn=0556-2805 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.2.754 | pages=754–772| bibcode=1970PhRvB...2..754A }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last=Litvin | first=D. B. | title=Ferroic classifications extended to ferrotoroidic crystals | journal=Acta Crystallographica Section A | publisher=International Union of Crystallography (IUCr) | volume=64 | issue=2 | date=2008-02-19 | issn=0108-7673 | doi=10.1107/s0108767307068262 | pages=316–320| pmid=18285626 | bibcode=2008AcCrA..64..316L }}</ref>

==Applications and extensions==

The main application of these space groups is to magnetic structure, where the black/white lattice points correspond to spin up/spin down configuration of [[electron spin]]. More abstractly, the magnetic space groups are often thought of as representing [[time reversal symmetry]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Electrodynamics of Continuous Media|author1=Lev Landau|author-link1=Lev Landau|author2=Evgeny Lifshitz|author-link2=Evgeny Lifshitz|series=A Course of Theoretical Physics|volume=8|pages=[https://archive.org/details/ElectrodynamicsOfContinuousMedia/page/n126 116]–119|publisher=Pergamon Press|year=1960|url=https://archive.org/details/ElectrodynamicsOfContinuousMedia|isbn=978-0-7506-2634-7}}</ref> This is in contrast to [[time crystal]]s, which instead have [[time translation symmetry]]. In the most general form, magnetic space groups can represent symmetries of any two valued lattice point property, such as positive/negative electrical charge or the alignment of electric dipole moments. The magnetic space groups place restrictions on the [[electronic band structure]] of materials. Specifically, they place restrictions on the connectivity of the different electron bands, which in turn defines whether material has [[symmetry-protected topological order]]. Thus, the magnetic space groups can be used to identify topological materials, such as [[topological insulator]]s.<ref>{{cite journal| last1=Elcoro | first1 = Luis | last2= Wieder | first2= Benjamin J. | last3 = Song | first3 = Zhida | last4 = Xu | first4 = Yuanfeng | last5 = Bradlyn | first5 = Barry | last6 = Bernevig | first6 = B. Andrei | title=Magnetic Topological Quantum Chemistry | journal=Nature Communications | publisher=Nature Research | volume=12 | page=5965 | year=2021 | issue = 1 | doi=10.1038/s41467-021-26241-8  | doi-access=free| pmid = 34645841 | pmc = 8514474 | arxiv=2010.00598 | bibcode = 2021NatCo..12.5965E }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Watanabe | first1=Haruki | last2=Po | first2=Hoi Chun | last3=Vishwanath | first3=Ashvin | title=Structure and topology of band structures in the 1651 magnetic space groups | journal=Science Advances | publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) | volume=4 | issue=8 | year=2018 | issn=2375-2548 | doi=10.1126/sciadv.aat8685 | article-number=eaat8685| pmid=30083612 | pmc=6070365 |arxiv=1707.01903| bibcode=2018SciA....4.8685W | s2cid=51910083 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Xu | first1= Yuanfeng | last2 = Elcoro | first2 = Luis | last3 = Song | first3 = Zhida | last4 = Wieder | first4 = Benjamin. J. | last5 = Vergniory | first5 = M. G. | last6 = Regnault | first6 = Nicolas | last7 = Chen | first7 = Yulin | last8 = Felser | first8 = Claudia | last9 = Bernevig | first9 = B. Andrei |title=High-throughput calculations of magnetic topological materials | journal= Nature | year = 2020 | volume= 586 | issue= 7831 | pages= 702–707 | doi= 10.1038/s41586-020-2837-0 | pmid= 33116291 | arxiv=2003.00012| bibcode= 2020Natur.586..702X | s2cid= 226036258 }}</ref>

Experimentally, the main source of information about magnetic space groups is [[neutron diffraction]] experiments. The resulting experimental profile can be matched to theoretical structures by [[Rietveld refinement]]<ref>{{cite journal | last=Rietveld | first=H. M. |author-link=Hugo Rietveld| title=A profile refinement method for nuclear and magnetic structures | journal=Journal of Applied Crystallography | publisher=International Union of Crystallography (IUCr) | volume=2 | issue=2 | date=1969-06-02 | issn=0021-8898 | doi=10.1107/s0021889869006558 | pages=65–71| bibcode=1969JApCr...2...65R }}</ref> or [[simulated annealing]].<ref>{{cite journal | last=Rodríguez-Carvajal | first=Juan | title=Recent advances in magnetic structure determination by neutron powder diffraction | journal=Physica B: Condensed Matter | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=192 | issue=1–2 | year=1993 | issn=0921-4526 | doi=10.1016/0921-4526(93)90108-i | pages=55–69| bibcode=1993PhyB..192...55R }}</ref>

Adding the two-valued symmetry is also a useful concept for [[frieze group]]s which are often used to classify artistic patterns. In that case, the 7 frieze groups with the addition of color reversal become 24 color-reversing frieze groups.<ref>{{cite conference|url=http://archive.bridgesmathart.org/2003/bridges2003-135.pdf|author1=David A. James|author2=Loukas N. Kalisperis|author3=Alice V. James|title=The Mathematics of Color-Reversing Decorative Friezes: Faaçdes of Pirgí, Greece|publisher=The International Society of the Arts, Mathematics, and Architecture|conference=Bridges: Mathematical Connections in Art, Music, and Science|year=2003|page=135}}</ref> Beyond the simple two-valued property, the idea has been extended further to two different types of antisymmetry ([[multiple antisymmetry]]),<ref name="Padmanabhan2020">Padmanabhan, H., Munro, J. M., Dabo, I and Gopalan, V. (2020). ''Antisymmetry: fundamentals and applications'', Annual Review of Materials Research, '''50''', 255–281, {{doi|10.1146/annurev-matsci-100219-101404}}</ref> to three colors in three dimensions,<ref name="Harker1981">{{cite journal|last1=Harker|first1=D.|title=The three-colored three-dimensional space groups|journal=Acta Crystallographica Section A|volume=37|issue=3|year=1981|pages=286–292|issn=0567-7394|doi=10.1107/S0567739481000697|bibcode=1981AcCrA..37..286H}}</ref> and to even higher dimensions and [[Polychromatic symmetry|more colors]].<ref>{{cite book|editor1=A. S. Marfunin|last1=Koptsik|first1=V. A.|title=General Results of Crystal Structure Analysis of Minerals|year=1994|pages=50–55|publisher=Springer Verlag Berlin Heidelberg|isbn=978-3-642-78525-2}}</ref>
